title: Swap the Patients
subtitle: one clinic's curve, everyone's patients

status: DRAFT: script under review together with its animatic.

segments.visual: Last time's ratio axis with two markers: Alder at 1.62, Dune at 1.46.

sentences.text: Last time, Alder's ratio came out at 1.62, and Dune's at 1.46. So Alder looks the worse of the two.
sentences.say: Last time, Alder's ratio came out at one point six two, and Dune's at one point four six. So Alder looks the worse of the two.

segments.visual: The probability panel with Alder's and Dune's curves. Dune's is the higher at both risk levels: 36% against 34%, and 81% against 80%. A lens magnifies the gap between them.

sentences.text: But put their curves side by side. Dune's is the higher one, at every level of risk.
Whoever you are, your chance of readmission is greater at Dune.

segments.visual: A question beside the curves: the higher curve, but the smaller ratio?

sentences.text: So how did Alder end up with the bigger ratio?
The answer is in who each clinic treats. And it leads to a second way of measuring.

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: swap the patients.

segments.visual: A grid of risk chips. The lower-risk column: 18% at the reference, 34% at Alder, 36% at Dune, with the multiples × 1.9 and × 2.0.

sentences.text: Start with lower-risk patients. At the reference, their chance is 18%. At Alder it is 34%, and at Dune, 36.
sentences.say: Start with lower-risk patients. At the reference, their chance is eighteen percent. At Alder it is thirty-four percent, and at Dune, thirty-six.

sentences.text: At either clinic, that is close to double.

segments.visual: The higher-risk column: 62%, 80% and 81%, with the multiples × 1.3 and × 1.3.

sentences.text: Now the higher-risk patients: 62% at the reference, 80 at Alder, 81 at Dune.
sentences.say: Now the higher-risk patients: sixty-two percent at the reference, eighty at Alder, eighty-one at Dune.

sentences.text: A much smaller multiple, about 1.3. It is Episode 5 again: the same gap in odds means less, in proportion, when the risk is already high.
sentences.say: A much smaller multiple, about one point three. It is Episode five again: the same gap in odds means less, in proportion, when the risk is already high.

segments.visual: Under the grid, who each clinic treats: Alder, 24 lower-risk and 6 higher-risk; Dune, 6 and 6. Beside them, their ratios: 1.62 and 1.46.

sentences.text: Here is the catch. Of Alder's 30 patients, 24 are lower-risk, where the multiple is near 2. Dune's 12 are split evenly.
sentences.say: Here is the catch. Of Alder's thirty patients, twenty-four are lower-risk, where the multiple is near two. Dune's twelve are split evenly.

sentences.text: So Alder's ratio is the larger because of who Alder treats, not because its curve is higher.

segments.visual: Dune's curve with Alder's patients: 1.68, above Alder's 1.62.

sentences.text: Give Dune Alder's patients, and Dune's ratio would be 1.68.
sentences.say: Give Dune Alder's patients, and Dune's ratio would be one point six eight.

sentences.text: Last time's ratio judges each clinic on its own patients. It does not line clinics up against one another.

segments.visual: Two small pictures: last time, a clinic's own patients on the reference curve; today, everyone's patients on the clinic's own curve. Then everyone as chips in clinic colours: 57 lower-risk, 46 higher-risk.

sentences.text: So turn last time's method around. Keep each clinic's curve, and swap the patients.
Give every clinic the same crowd: all 103 patients in the cast. 57 lower-risk, 46 higher-risk.
sentences.say: Give every clinic the same crowd: all one hundred and three patients in the cast. Fifty-seven lower-risk, forty-six higher-risk.

segments.visual: Alder's curve on the probability panel, with two large risk chips: 57 patients at 34%, 46 at 80%. The sum: 57 × 0.343 + 46 × 0.796 = 56.2. Then 56.2 of 103 = 54.5%.

sentences.text: Under Alder's curve, that is 57 patients at 34%, and 46 at 80%. Add up the chances: 56.2 readmissions.
sentences.say: Under Alder's curve, that is fifty-seven patients at thirty-four percent, and forty-six at eighty percent. Add up the chances: fifty-six point two readmissions.

sentences.text: 56.2 out of 103. If everyone had gone to Alder, the model expects 54.5% to be readmitted.
sentences.say: Fifty-six point two out of one hundred and three. If everyone had gone to Alder, the model expects fifty-four point five percent to be readmitted.

segments.visual: A label: Alder's direct rate. One clinic's curve, everyone's patients.

sentences.text: That is Alder's direct rate. One clinic's curve, everyone's patients.

scenes.chapter: The same patients, at every clinic

segments.visual: Five bars: 54.5%, 32.2%, 37.6%, 55.9%, and Elm's 0.7%. Beside Alder and Dune, last time's ratios, 1.62 and 1.46, for contrast.

sentences.text: Now every clinic. Alder, 54.5%. Birch, 32.2. Cedar, 37.6. Dune, 55.9.
sentences.say: Now every clinic. Alder, fifty-four point five percent. Birch, thirty-two point two. Cedar, thirty-seven point six. Dune, fifty-five point nine.

sentences.text: And Dune is back above Alder. On the same patients, the higher curve always gives the higher rate.

segments.visual: Elm's bar is hatched, with a note: 0.74% or 0.004%, depending on where the fitting stopped.

sentences.text: Elm's figure, 0.7%, is hatched. It rests on a gamma that only records where the fitting stopped.
sentences.say: Elm's figure, zero point seven percent, is hatched. It rests on a gamma that only records where the fitting stopped.

segments.visual: Two vertical lines across the bars: the overall rate, 40.8%, marked as not the yardstick; and the reference clinic's rate, 37.6%. A note: 38.8 readmissions, as last time.

sentences.text: One trap. The overall rate was 41%, but that is not the yardstick here. Cedar, the reference clinic itself, comes out at 37.6.
sentences.say: One trap. The overall rate was forty-one percent, but that is not the yardstick here. Cedar, the reference clinic itself, comes out at thirty-seven point six.

sentences.text: Everyone at the reference would have 38.8 readmissions, the same 38.8 we met last time. So compare a direct rate with the reference clinic's, not with the overall rate.
sentences.say: Everyone at the reference would have thirty-eight point eight readmissions, the same thirty-eight point eight we met last time. So compare a direct rate with the reference clinic's, not with the overall rate.

segments.visual: 54.5 ÷ 37.6 = 1.45, beside last time's 1.62.

sentences.text: Against Cedar's 37.6, Alder's 54.5 is 1.45 times as high. Last time's ratio said 1.62.
sentences.say: Against Cedar's thirty-seven point six, Alder's fifty-four point five is one point four five times as high. Last time's ratio said one point six two.

sentences.text: Both are right. They answer different questions.

segments.visual: The left card: this clinic, the patients it treated. Under it: holding a clinic to account.

sentences.text: Last time's question: how did this clinic do with the patients it actually treated? That is the one to ask when a clinic is held to account.

segments.visual: The right card: this clinic, everyone's patients. Under it: choosing between clinics. Across both: neither is a rate anyone experienced.

sentences.text: Today's question: how would this clinic do with everyone's patients? That is closer to what someone choosing between clinics wants to know.
And neither is a rate that anyone actually experienced.

scenes.chapter: The price of a common footing

segments.visual: Alder: treated 24 lower-risk and 6 higher-risk patients; asked about 57 and 46. A bar for its 56.2: 19.5 from lower-risk patients, 36.6 from higher-risk.

sentences.text: A common footing has a price. Alder treated only 6 higher-risk patients. Its direct rate asks its curve about 46.
sentences.say: A common footing has a price. Alder treated only six higher-risk patients. Its direct rate asks its curve about forty-six.

sentences.text: Two-thirds of that 56.2 comes from patients of a kind Alder hardly saw.
sentences.say: Two-thirds of that fifty-six point two comes from patients of a kind Alder hardly saw.

segments.visual: Elm: treated 11 and 0; asked about 57 and 46. A note: all of it rests on curves of one shape.

sentences.text: For Elm it is starker. Elm treated no higher-risk patients at all. Its figure rests entirely on the model's assumption that every clinic's curve has the same shape.

segments.visual: The crowd: each provider's ratio from last time against today's. A tight band, with four providers ringed: they move ten places or more between the two rankings.

sentences.text: In the crowd of 200, the two measures agree closely. Yet between the two rankings, four providers move ten places or more.
sentences.say: In the crowd of two hundred, the two measures agree closely. Yet between the two rankings, four providers move ten places or more.

sentences.text: A ranking can shift with the question, before luck has even entered.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Last time: a clinic's own patients, on the reference curve.
This time: everyone's patients, on the clinic's own curve.
The second compares like with like, but asks each clinic about patients it never treated. Always say which one you are reporting.

segments.visual: Alder's 13 against 8.02, large; the next episode's title.

sentences.text: One question is still open. Alder had 13 readmissions where the reference expects 8. A real difference, or luck?
sentences.say: One question is still open. Alder had thirteen readmissions where the reference expects eight. A real difference, or luck?

sentences.text: Next time: unequal coins.
